newsitem.title: USA: Kansas wheat yields better than expected - dealers.
newsitem.headline: Kansas wheat yields better than expected - dealers.

text.p: Kansas wheat yields continue to improve and are in some cases coming in between 50 and 70 bushels an acre, compared to the state-wide average of 29 bushels in 1996, Kansas wheat dealers and crop experts said.
"In central, northwestern and eastern parts of the state, we have seen much better-than-expected yields," said Ray Lamond, soil fertility extension specialist with Kansas State University.
"It's not uncommon to see 70 to 80 bushels per acre in some areas. But the average for the state may run 40 to 45 bushels or better," Lamond said.
"We had areas where there was no problem with the freeze," Lamond said, referring to a hard freeze that hit the hard red winter wheat crop in mid-April.

"I think what is making the exceptional yield is a longer grain filling period that we usually have," he said. "From mid-April to June, we had cool nights and low humidity, which retarded disease development."
A dealer in southcentral Kansas agreed that ideal weather after the April freeze had boosted crop growth.

"We had cool but not cold weather. We had good moisture spaced out across the time frame which really kicked those secondary tillers in and had them catch up to replace a lot of the damaged wheat," the merchandiser told Reuters on Friday.
He noted the part of the state that was hit the hardest was the southwestern corner where the April freeze caused significant damage to tillers.
Test weights have been good, except for the southwest corner where some fields have had light test weights.
Across the state they are 55 to 63 (lbs per bushel)" with the low numbers from southwest and Oklahoma Panhandle, he said.
A good test weight would be 60 lbs per bushel or higher, said Curtis Thompson, Kansas State crop and soil extension specialist in Garden City, Kan.
"Despite the significant freeze damage, we are still finding 40 to 50 bushel yields in some instances in the southwestern corner with some test weights up to 60 lbs," Thompson said.
Thompson, who covers 24 counties in southwestern Kansas, said, cutting was underway in every one of those counties.
Except for a few scattered showers Thursday and Friday in southern Kansas and Oklahoma, the HRW wheat area would be dry, allowing harvest to continue through the weekend.
"They have the next five days with pretty much no major (rain) delays, but after that they could have some problems," said Joel Burgio, meteorologist with Weather Services Corp.
